d: The deliberate act of delaying and playing instead of working
ety: From Middle English daliaunce et al., from dalien (“to exchange pleasantries, to chat; to flirt”), from Old French dalier, dailer. By surface analysis, dally + -ance.
s: He had passed the officer now. There was no necessity for dalliance. He pressed the accelerator down a trifle.

d: A person of refined upbringing and manners
ety: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian
s: The emperor elevated several loyal families to the status of patricians.

d: Generous in assistance to the poor
ety: From Medieval Latin eleēmosynārius (“alms dispenser”), from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē, “suffix denoting an abstract noun”). Compare Italian elemosina.
s: Crouch low thy neck to eleemosynary gifts.

d: Of something having a dusty purplish pink color
ety: From Middle English roseat, from Anglo-Latin roseātus, equivalent to rose + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
s: The countess took the roseate palm and snowy fingers of this lovely child.

d: A small gate in the rear of a fort or castle
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English postern, posterne (“side door or gate; small entranceway; hidden or secret door or passage”), from Late Latin posterna, and from its likely etymon Anglo-Norman posterne and Old French posterne (“hidden exit from a fortified building; back door; small door”) (modern French poterne), a variant of posterle (“back door or passage”) (although this is attested lat
s: In the outwork was a sally-port corresponding to the postern of the castle, and the whole was surrounded by a strong palisade.

d: Someone who insists on something
ety: From Middle English stighteler, stytelere, equivalent to stickle + -er. The judges at Cornish wrestling matches do indeed carry sticks which serve for signalling and as a badge of their office. This practice has evolved from holding swords and then swordsticks.
s: Lexicographers are sticklers for correct language.

d: A feeling of extreme pleasure or satisfaction
ety: Attested from the mid 14th century, from Old French delectation (“enjoyment”), from Latin dēlectātiōnem, accusative singular of dēlectātiō, from the verb Latin dēlectō (“to delight, charm, please”), frequentative of dēliciō, from de- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. By surface analysis, delect + -ation or delectate +
s: Do not let us men despise these instincts because we cannot feel them. These women were made for our comfort and delectation, gentlemen,—with all the rest of the minor animals.

d: Barely satisfying a lower standard
ety: From hard + scrabble.
s: He leads a hardscrabble existence.

d: A woman’s headscarf folded into a triangle and tied under the chin; worn by Russian peasant women
ety: Borrowed from Russian ба́бушка (bábuška, “grandmother”), from Old East Slavic бабушка (babuška, “grandmother, midwife”). First attested in the 1830s.
s: White Parian bust of smiling Russian peasant woman - with babushka covering head, lovely detail work, 21½″ tall

d: Lucky in making unexpected and fortunate discoveries
ety: From serendipity + -ous.
s: The weather was serendipitous for our vacation.

d: Convert to another faith or religion
ety: From proselyte + -ize.
s: “I am not sent here to proselytize. My church is not in that business.”

d: A natural disposition to be hostile
ety: From Latin pugnacitas (whence -acity).
s: His sister is out front, cleaning her gun with that intimidating pugnacity that has most of the men in town keeping well clear of her.

d: To make better
ety: First attested in 1542; borrowed from Late Latin meliorātus, perfect passive participle of meliorō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from melior (“better”).
s: They offered some compromises in an effort to meliorate the disagreement.

d: A dissolute man in fashionable society
ety: The adjective is first attested in 1535, the verb in 1542; borrowed from Latin prōflīgātus, perfect passive participle of prōflīgō (“to strike down, cast down”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 an 3) and pro-), from prō- (“forward”) + flīgō (“to strike, dash”) + -ō (1st conjugation compound verb-forming suffix). Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
s: Have you come to Nelson seeking your death, profligate?

d: Letter for letter
ety: From Medieval Latin litterātim, from littera (“letter”). First known use: 1643.
s: In order to give its Scots flavor to the eye, as I cannot to the ear, I shall transcribe its beginning literatim.

d: A trellis on which ornamental shrub or fruit tree is trained to grow flat
ety: Borrowed from French espalier, from Italian spalliera, from spalla (“shoulder”).
s: The garment stalls carried the traditional blue vine-dressers' outfits, sunhats, and the great willow pitchforks grown in espalier at villages like Sauve.

d: The outermost region of the sun’s atmosphere; visible as a white halo during a solar eclipse
ety: From Middle English aureole, from Old French aureole, from Medieval Latin aureola (corona) (“golden (crown)”). Doublet of oriole.
s: Those white women whose superiority encircled them like an aureole, could quieten any raucous gathering by just placing a finger to a lip.

d: Political propaganda (especially communist propaganda) communicated via art and literature and cinema
ety: The noun is borrowed from Russian агитпро́п (agitpróp, “agitprop”), Агитпро́п (Agitpróp, “Agitprop (Department for Agitation and Propaganda of the Soviet Union)”), short for отде́л агитации и пропаганды (otdél agitacii i propagandy, “Department for Agitation and Propaganda”); analysable as a blend of agitation + propaganda. The verb is derived from the noun.
s: Like most pieces of agitprop, the Lucas and Sargent paper vastly overstated the deficiencies of the old order.

d: A name given to a product or service
ety: Borrowed from French marque. Doublet of mark. Ultimately cognate with marquee.
s: The group wants Rover as its luxury marque and MG as the performance car.

d: An explanation or critical interpretation (especially of the Bible)
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “to explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead, guide”).
s: As with Deism and Materialism, the German Rationalism invaded the department of Biblical exegesis.

d: Martial music with variations; to be played by bagpipes
ety: From Scottish Gaelic pìobaireachd (“act of playing the bagpipes”), from pìobaire (“piper”) + -achd (“abstract noun suffix”).
s: Ever, as on they bore, more loud / And louder rung the pibroch proud.

d: Walking with a slow dragging motion without lifting your feet
ety: From Middle English schambyll, shamyll, schamel, from Old English sċeamol, scamol (“bench, stool”), from Proto-West Germanic *skamul, *skamil, from Proto-Germanic *skamulaz, *skamilaz, from Latin scamellum, a variant of scabellum (“footstool”). Cognate with West Frisian skammel (“shamble, trestle, stool", also (in the plural) "legs, especially when showing defects or deformities”), Dutch schemel (
s: From his shambling I assumed he was very old.

d: Someone who appreciates wine
ety: From oeno- + -phile.
s: The oenophile had a large wine cellar stocked with bottles from around the world.

d: Manual dexterity in the execution of tricks
ety: From French prestidigitation, from French preste (“nimble, quick”) + Latin digitus (“finger”) + French -ation (process suffix). The word has a different origin from prestige, even though this in the past has meant “delusion, illusion, trick”.
s: My favorite prestidigitation was when he pulled the live dove out of that tiny scarf.

d: A triangular board supported on casters; when lightly touched with the fingertips it is supposed to spell out supernatural (or unconscious) messages
ety: Borrowed from French planchette. By surface analysis, French planche + -ette.
s: Some general security features to look for in both Canadian and American currency are . . .small green dots or "planchettes" randomly embedded throughout the paper that glow under ultraviolet light.

d: Floor consisting of open space at the top of a house just below roof; often used for storage
ety: From Middle English garett, garite, from Old French garite, guerite (“watchtower”), from garir, guarir (“to defend, protect”) (compare English garrison), ultimately of Germanic origin (see English garage). Doublet of guerite.
s: While a boon to garret-living, financially struggling young musicians, the library has caught the attention of music publishers.

d: Of visual imagery of almost photographic accuracy
ety: From German eidetisch, from Ancient Greek εἰδητικός (eidētikós), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”).
s: ‘Funny that I should remember it? I have an eidetic memory for numbers, can't help

d: Tending to diminish or disparage
ety: From deprecate + -ory.
s: Said the Duke, bowing over a deprecatory hand, “If there were to pass my window one tithe of them whose hearts have been lost to Miss Dobson, I should win no solace from that interminable parade.”

d: Habitually disposed to disobedience and opposition
ety: From Middle English froward, fraward, equivalent to fro + -ward. Compare Old English fromweard, framweard (“turned away, having the back turned”).
s: ‘I owe much to Éomer,’ said Théoden. ‘Faithful heart may have froward tongue.’

d: The lowest brass wind instrument
ety: Named after American composer and conductor John Philip Sousa + -phone.
s: One version of the large tuba, popular in marching bands, is called a sousaphone in honor of bandsman John Philip Sousa.

d: A short literary or musical composition
ety: From French morceau, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, past participle of mordeō, mordēre (“bite, nibble, gnaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to rub, wipe; to pack, rob”). Doublet of morsel.
s: M. De Luc has a specimen of the uranite (Peckblend) mixed with titan and crystals of quartz, a morceau of singular beauty

d: The style in which newspapers are written
ety: From journal + -ese.
s: We write journalese out of habit, sometimes from misguided training, and to sound urgent, authoritative and, well, journalistic. But it doesn't do any of that.

d: A bold outlaw (especially on the American frontier)
ety: From obsolete Spanish desperado, past participle of desperar, archaic form of desesperar (“to despair”), from Latin disperare (“to despair, to lose hope”), from prefix dis- + sperare (“to hope”). Doublet of desperate.
s: Surely this was the face of a desperado.

d: From that time on
ety: From Middle English thennesforth, equivalent to thence + forth.
s: Here his hand trembled as he set his pen to the proclamation that declared slaves thenceforth and forever free.

d: Defying imitation; matchless
ety: Borrowed from Middle French inimitable, from Latin inimitabilis, corresponding to in- + imitable.
s: Let's see you pay for your drink in your own inimitable fashion, huh? A song, Denton! How about it?

d: A sheer stiff muslin
ety: From French organdi, possibly derived from the French name of the city Urgench.
s: Beside them stood a puzzled female dwarf with a hideously rouged face as if ready for the circus; she was clad in white organdie with a marriage veil.

d: Burst or split open
ety: Borrowed from Latin dehīscō (“to gape, open”), from hiō (“to be open”); related to hiatus.
s: Anthers dehisce when the flower opens.

d: Someone who is no longer alive
ety: From Latin decedens, present active participle of decedere (“to depart, die”).
s: “A check of the nightstands revealed large amounts of prescription medication in the decedent’s name,” the coroner’s notes said, according to TMZ.com.

d: An act of plundering and pillaging and marauding
ety: From Middle French déprédation, from Latin depraedatio.
s: Depredation of cultivated crops by elephants is widespread in both Africa and Asia.

d: Wicked and cruel behavior
ety: Variant of devilry, influenced by gallantry.
s: They stand back to make room for every rascal and demagogue who chooses to cloak his selfish deviltry under the veil of race pride.
